summary_paragraph: A man with a history of non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 20%), type 2 diabetes, COPD, schizophrenia, and cocaine use was admitted for acute decompensation of systolic heart failure following recent crack use. He presented with worsening shortness of breath, orthopnea, and productive cough. Initial treatment with IV furosemide showed limited response, prompting transfer to cardiology and a trial of IV lasix drip, which led to significant fluid loss and symptom improvement. Due to poor oral absorption, he was transitioned to torsemide 60 mg daily. His diabetes was complicated by hypoglycemia, requiring reduction and subsequent adjustment of insulin glargine. Cocaine use was directly linked to the decompensation, and he was referred to an addiction program and psychiatry for ongoing support. He stabilized, lost weight, and was discharged home with close follow-up, strict instructions to avoid cocaine and sodium, and a plan to monitor daily weights.
